lon_001: You can recognise it by the hollow trunk, propped up and nearly eight metres round, cut back hard by repeated pollarding. It stands in St Andrew's churchyard at Totteridge, older by a thousand years than the church beside it.
lon_002: You can recognise it by the huge hollow pollard trunk, split and gnarled and wide enough to shelter a small football team. It stands near Pen Ponds in Richmond Park, usually with fallow deer grazing around it.
lon_003: You can recognise it by the buildings beside it, held to two storeys by their leases so its crown keeps open sky. It stands on the corner of Wood Street and Cheapside, in the churchyard of a church that burned in 1666.
lon_004: You can recognise it by there being more than thirty of them, planted together in 1789 as one scheme, which is why this entry marks the square rather than a single trunk. It stands in the railed garden of Mayfair's Berkeley Square.
lon_005: You can recognise it by the thickened, part hollow trunk of a sweet chestnut, pollarded more than once, and by the spiny green cases it drops across the grass every October. It stands in the Flower Garden of Greenwich Park.
lon_006: You can recognise it by the wooden props holding it up and by the lean that brings its lower branches almost to the grass. It stands in the garden of Charlton House, the Jacobean mansion now used as a community centre.
lon_007: You can recognise it by its evergreen leaves, a Mediterranean holm oak still in leaf when its neighbours are bare, and by the low base it was once coppiced to. It stands in Fulham Palace Gardens, free and open daily.
lon_008: You can recognise it by the small Great Trees of London plaque at its foot, which calls it simply the oldest plane in London. It stands at Barn Elms, on the edge of the land beside the London Wetland Centre.
lon_009: You can recognise it by the small marker naming it one of the Old Lions: the Japanese pagoda tree planted in 1762, the most storied of Kew's five oldest survivors. It stands inside Kew Gardens, which charges entry.
lon_010: You can recognise it by the fence around it and the stone marker at its base telling the wheelbarrow story about Peter the Great. It stands propped in Sayes Court Park in Deptford, where nothing else of the garden survives.
lon_013: You can recognise it by the roots, risen clear of the ground in ridges across the forecourt with the hotel's garden tucked underneath them. It stands on The Dorchester's forecourt on Park Lane, in view from the pavement.
lon_014: You can recognise it by its height, more than 100 feet by the Great Trees map, and by the way it leans out over the pavement toward the road. It stands outside the Memorial Garden of Rest on Marylebone High Street.
lon_015: You can recognise it by being the odd one out, an Oriental Plane rather than the London Planes on the streets around it, and by its size, one of the largest on that corner. It stands where Horse Guards Avenue meets the Embankment.
lon_016: You can recognise it by the information board beside it and by its size, the one very large plane in a small square. It stands in Brunswick Square Gardens in Bloomsbury, with the Foundling Museum on the far side.
lon_018: You can recognise it by the swollen, knobbled trunk under a crown far too small for it. It stands south of the lower grassy area in Ravenscourt Park, near the elm avenue, about 150 metres from the park's tree of heaven.
lon_023: You can recognise it by the circular green plaque at its foot naming it a Great Tree of London and one of the largest of its species in the country. It stands by the sports area and playground in Ravenscourt Park.
